blocks.text: What OTC Medications Can I Take and Still Be Safe to Fly?
blocks.html: What OTC Medications Can I Take and Still Be Safe to Fly?

blocks.text: 1. First, ask yourself “Do I have an underlying condition that makes me unsafe to fly?”
blocks.html: 1. First, ask yourself “Do I have an underlying condition that makes me unsafe to fly?”

blocks.text: Title 14 CFR 61.53 is the regulation, which prohibits fight with a known medical deficiency (unless cleared by the FAA) and requires that you determine that you are ft to fly prior to each fight.
blocks.html: Title 14 CFR 61.53 is the regulation, which prohibits fight with a known medical deficiency (unless cleared by the FAA) and requires that you determine that you are ft to fly prior to each fight.

blocks.text:
- Am I sick?
- Am I having trouble clearing my ears at ground level?
- Do I feel bad enough that I keep thinking about how I feel?
- Are others asking me if I am ok?
- Do I feel good enough to fly ONLY if I take medication?
- Am I getting worse?

blocks.text: 2. Next, consider these issues before operating an aircraft:
blocks.html: 2. Next, consider these issues before operating an aircraft:

blocks.text:
- In the last few days, have you taken, or do you plan to take any medications before flying?
- If currently taking a medication only for symptom relief, would you be safe to fly without it?
- Do you have any other underlying health conditions?
- Discuss these conditions with your AME or family physician to determine if you are safe to fly.
- Specifically ask about your ability “to operate machinery” (including any aircraft).
- Discuss if the medication, OTC or otherwise, will pose a problem with the underlying condition or other health conditions and/or other medications that you are taking.
blocks.html:
• In the last few days, have you taken, or do you plan to take any medications before flying?
  • If currently taking a medication only for symptom relief, would you be safe to fly without it?
  • Do you have any other underlying health conditions?
  • Discuss these conditions with your AME or family physician to determine if you are safe to fly.
  • Specifically ask about your ability “to operate machinery” (including any aircraft).
  • Discuss if the medication, OTC or otherwise, will pose a problem with the underlying condition or other health conditions and/or other medications that you are taking.

blocks.text: 3. When choosing an OTC Medication, follow these steps:
blocks.html: 3. When choosing an OTC Medication, follow these steps:

blocks.text: 4. NO GO Medications:
blocks.html: 4. NO GO Medications:

blocks.text: If you take any of the NO GO medications listed in the OTC Medications Reference Table OR if you have previously had side effects from the medication, wait at least five (5) dosage intervals after the last dose before flying. See examples on the following page of dosage interval wait time for the recommended grounding period after discontinuation of the medication.

blocks.text: Always follow 14 CFR 61.53. If it is not familiar to you, please review it. Not only is it a requirement, but it is for your safety and that of your passengers.
blocks.html: Always follow 14 CFR 61.53. If it is not familiar to you, please review it. Not only is it a requirement, but it is for your safety and that of your passengers.

blocks.text: When in doubt, SAFETY FIRST - DO NOT FLY.
blocks.html: When in doubt, SAFETY FIRST - DO NOT FLY.

blocks.text:
- Do one more check of your condition before considering flying.
- Get well before considering return to fight status. Do not push it.
- Remember, OTC medications help reduce the symptoms of an illness, but do not cure it.
- Even though a medication has been determined to be safe for use by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), this does not mean that the medication is compatible with flying or even driving.
- If you choose to fly on medication, be certain that it will not impair safety. Do not simply hope for the best.
